This guide helps you choose an appropriate spatial statistic to answer the question you want to ask.
Each section below names one question. It then gives the function, the input, and how to understand the results.

A few definitions:
A *spot* is spatially-resolved location where we capture gene expression or a BCR/TCR sequence.
A *clone* is a group of cells that are inferred to descend from a common ancestor.
*Spatial autocorrelation* is the tendency of nearby spots to have similar values, i.e., high values by
high values and low values by low values.

All tests need a SIRUP object, or a Seurat object with spatial images. The tests read the spot
coordinates from the object. Most tests compare each spot with its "neighbors". Generally, you can set the
number of neighbors with `k` (i.e., the `k` nearest spots will be neighbors) or `radius` (which draws a 
circle with radius `radius` around the point in question and all points inside that circle are neighbors of the point).


## Match the question to the function

| Question | Function | Input |
|---|---|---|
| Is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Where is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialLocalMoran()` | One gene or numeric metadata column |
| Do two continuous variables co-vary in space? | `spatialLee()` | Two continuous variables |
| How far does a clone spread? | `spatialCloneSpread()` | Receptor table with clone IDs, pass the ID of the clone you're interested in |
| Is a discrete variable (in this case a particular clone) spatially autocorrelated? | `spatialCloneJoinCount()` | Receptor table with clone IDs, pass the ID of the clone you're interested in |
| Do two discrete variables co-vary in space? | `spatialRipleyCrossK()` | One metadata column with two labels |


## Is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialMoran()` to determine if a continuous variable is spatially autocorrelated, i.e., if 
neighboring spots have similar values. This function computes [Moran's I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moran%27s_I#Global_Moran's_I).
Moran's I is near 0 when the values show no spatial pattern, it is positive when similar values are nearby, and
it is negative when dissimilar values are nearby.

The input is a SIRUP or Seurat object. `variable_type` tells the function what type of variable it is: a gene (`"feature"`) or
a numeric metadata column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The estimate $I$ and the associated p value are reported. Note that a larger section can 
inflate significance, so you may see a tiny p value for a weak pattern in larger datasets.

See the code below for an example on a synthetic object.

```{r moran}
library(SIRUP)
x <- readSIRUP(system.file("extdata", "sirup_synthetic.rds", package = "SIRUP"))
moran <- spatialMoran(x, variable = "gene1", variable_type = "feature", k = 4)
moran$test$estimate[[1]]
moran$test$p.value
```

## **Where** is a continuous variable spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialLocalMoran()` to find where a continuous variable is spatially autocorrelated, i.e., which spots
sit in a cluster of similar values. This function computes [local Moran's I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moran%27s_I#Local_Moran's_I)
(also called LISA) for each spot. Local Moran's I is positive when a spot has neighbors with similar values
and negative when a spot differs from its neighbors.

The input is a SIRUP or Seurat object. `variable_type` tells the function what type of variable it is: a gene (`"feature"`) or
a numeric metadata column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The result has one row for each spot, with the local I (`local_i`), a z-score (`z_i`), and a p value (`p_value`). Each spot has its
own p value, so we should adjust for multiple testing. `plotSpatialLocalMoran()` draws the z-scores on the tissue.

See the code below for an example on a synthetic object.

```{r local-moran}
local_moran <- spatialLocalMoran(x, variable = "gene1", variable_type = "feature", k = 4)
head(local_moran[, c("cell", "local_i", "z_i", "p_value")])
plotSpatialLocalMoran(x, local_moran)
```

## Do two continuous variables co-vary in space?

Use `spatialLee()` to determine if two continuous variables share a spatial pattern, i.e., if a high value of one
variable tends to sit near high values of the other. This function computes [Lee's L](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%27s_L).
Lee's L is near 0 when the variables show no shared pattern, it is positive when
both variables are high (or both low) in the same neighborhoods, and it is negative when one variable is high where the other is low.

The input is a SIRUP object or a Seurat object. `x` and `y` are the names of the two variables, and
`x_type` and `y_type` tell the function what type each variable is: a gene (`"feature"`) or
a numeric metadata column (`"metadata"`). `k` is the number of neighbors.

The estimate $L$ and the associated p value are reported. The default test (`method = "analytical"`) builds a dense matrix with one entry for
each pair of spots, so it needs a lot of memory for large datasets. For large data, such as Visium HD, set `method = "mc"` to use
a permutation test.

See the code below for an example on a synthetic object.

```{r lee}
lee <- spatialLee(x, x = "gene1", x_type = "feature", y = "gene2", y_type = "feature", k = 4)
lee$L
lee$test$p.value
```

## How far does a clone spread?

Use `spatialCloneSpread()` to determine how far clones spread across the tissue, i.e., how far apart their
or sequences are. This function is just descriptive. For each clone, it
computes the distance between every pair of points and reports the mean and the maximum of those distances.

The input is a SIRUP object or receptor table with clone IDs and spatial IDs. A clone needs at least `min_spatial_ids`
points (default 2). By default, each sequence is a point, so sequences in the same spot give distances of 0. Set
`collapse_within_spot = TRUE` to count each spot once.

The result has one row for each sample and clone, with the number of spots (`n_spatial_ids`), the mean distance
(`mean_pairwise_distance`), and the maximum distance (`max_pairwise_distance`). Distances are in image pixels.

See the code below for an example on a synthetic object.

```{r spread}
spatialCloneSpread(x)
```

## Is a discrete variable (i.e., a particular clone) spatially autocorrelated?

Use `spatialCloneJoinCount()` to determine if a discrete variable is spatially autocorrelated. This function computes
the [join count statistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Join_count_statistic). Here, the variable is
whether a spot holds a particular clone, i.e., if the spots of a clone sit next to each other. This function marks the spots that hold the
clone, counts the neighbor pairs in which both spots hold the clone (the joins), and compares that count with the count expected by chance.
The observed count is higher than expected when the sequences in the clone stay nearby each other.

The input is a SIRUP object receptor table with clone IDs and spatial IDs. By default, the function tests every clone that
occurs in at least `min_spatial_ids` spots. Give `clone_val` to test chosen clones. If the object has stored polygons, the function runs one
test for each polygon. Set `use_stored_polygons = FALSE` to run one test over the entire section in this case.

The `summary` table has one row for each clone, with the observed and expected join counts, a z-score (`statistic`), and a p value (`p_value`). The
default alternative is `"greater"`, so the test looks for more joins than chance. The function tests many clones at once, so be sure
to adjust for multiple testing.

See the code below for an example on a synthetic object.

```{r join-count}
join_count <- spatialCloneJoinCount(x, use_stored_polygons = FALSE, k = 4)
join_count$summary[, c("clone_id", "observed_join_count", "expected_join_count", "p_value")]
```

## Do two discrete variables co-vary in space?

Use `spatialRipleyCrossK()` to determine if two discrete variables co-vary in space, i.e., if spots of type A lie
near spots of type B. This function computes [Ripley's cross K](https://academicweb.nd.edu/~mhaenggi/ee87021/Dixon-K-Function.pdf?utm_campaign=redirect&utm_medium=web&utm_source=www3.nd.edu). It counts the spots of type B within each distance of an average
spot of type A. It then compares that curve with curves from random relabeling of the spots, which gives an envelope. 
Ripley's cross K is similar to Lee's L, but it works with discrete data rather than continuous.

The input is a SIRUP object or a Seurat object with a column that holds the labels (`mark_col`). 
Give the two levels to compare as `i` and `j`. Set `nsim` above 0 to generate the randomly relabeled envelope
for comparison. Spots with `NA` in the column are left out.

The result holds the observed K at each distance (`plot_data`). A curve above the envelope means that A and B sit closer than chance, i.e., they **colocalize**. A curve
below the envelope means that A and B are. `plotRipleyCrossK()` draws the curve and the envelope. The distance is in image pixels at the
stored `image_scale`.

See the code below for an example on a synthetic object.

```{r ripley, eval = has_spatstat}
set.seed(1)
kcross <- spatialRipleyCrossK(x, mark_col = "cell_type", i = "A", j = "B", nsim = 19)
plotRipleyCrossK(kcross)
```
